title: Tiers, add-ons and one expansion lever at a time
decision_task: How to structure tiers and add-ons, and which lever to add when a single flat offer leaves no room for customers to pay more as they get more value.
applies_when: One flat price for everyone, little or no expansion revenue
Best customers clearly get more value than others
A new capability is launching and the owner asks whether to include it or charge for it
exclusions: Customer count too small to tell segments apart (start with one offer plus one add-on)
Tier differences would gate something the entry plan needs to deliver its promise
Operating more packages would overload support or billing
evidence_requirements: Segments with different jobs or willingness to pay (interviews, purchase data)
Which features or services customers name as the reason they buy
Adoption timing of features after purchase
missing_data_behavior: No plan-choice data: one offer plus one add-on; uptake assumptions labelled.
Segments can't be told apart: don't add tiers.
alternatives_when_constrained: Low traffic: offer the premium option in sales conversations and log acceptance before publishing
Service business: premium = faster turnaround or priority access; add-on = optional extra service
No billing integration: separate invoice line items

decision_branches.if: Most buyers pick the middle and the top tier is near zero
decision_branches.then: Revisit tier boundaries before adding anchors.

decision_branches.if: A capability helps only some customers and isn't needed for the core promise
The entry plan can't deliver its own promise
decision_branches.then: Move the capability down; don't gate it.

implementation_steps: Write one sentence per plan: who it is for and why they buy
Default to three tiers when segments differ; one offer when they don't
Run the add-on test for each capability: polarising, different buyer/budget, replaces another vendor, adopted later, or costly to serve
Limit first purchase to one or two add-ons
Pick one expansion lever to test: premium tier, paid add-on, usage limit by tier, lite access level, minimum team size, or a disclosed annual escalator on new contracts
Fold proven add-ons into a higher tier periodically to keep the lineup simple
dependencies: Billing that supports add-ons or tiers

cash_and_labor_requirements.cash: None to test on new buyers
cash_and_labor_requirements.labor: Owner 2-3 h; support load per extra plan

metrics: Revenue per customer and contribution per customer
Downgrades and cannibalisation from top tier
guardrails: Entry plan must deliver its advertised outcome
Escalators disclosed at signup, applied only per contract terms
Existing customers' terms unchanged during tests (PB-pricing-test)
observation_window: At least one full renewal or repurchase cycle; 8–12 weeks of new signups for uptake reads, longer at low volume.
stop_conditions: Premium uptake well below plan and base conversion falls: rethink tier boundaries
Add-on causes billing confusion or complaints: bundle it
More than two add-ons routinely needed: repackage
review_triggers: Owner corrects an input this playbook relies on
A metric or guardrail crosses its bound
The underlying source or platform rule changes
climbos_location: Pricing page advice, plan engine offer stage, PB-pricing-test (versioned variant: 'add an expansion lever'), Climb AI packaging Q&A, revenue calculator.

interpretation: Interpretation: the add-on test is the most transferable piece for small businesses; numeric uptake and pricing ratios are software heuristics to use only as starting assumptions.
proposed_climbos_rule: Proposed ClimbOS rule: every package recommendation states each plan's buyer and reason in one sentence, passes the add-on test for each extra, and shows expansion revenue as uptake × price difference with owner-supplied or clearly labelled assumed uptake.
disagreements: BK02 Ch 11 treats a middle tier as a compromise-effect tactic; GU-02 warns everyone defaulting to the middle can be a symptom of arbitrary plans. Decide by plan-choice data: if most buyers choose the middle and the top tier sees near-zero uptake, revisit boundaries rather than adding anchors.

hypothetical_evaluation_cases.label: hypothetical

inputs_hypothetical.observation: a third of clients ask for payroll and monthly calls

expected_behavior: Suggests payroll as an add-on (different need, costly to serve) or a premium tier with calls
Computes revenue lift as uptake × price difference using owner assumptions labelled hypothetical
Keeps base package delivering full bookkeeping
Labels the 15–25% uptake range as one author's software experience
hard_failure: Moving core bookkeeping into the premium tier
Promising Kyle's +15% revenue as an expected result

notes: Proposed reference contract. Not executable; does not authorize publishing, sending or spending. Numbers in source references are dated author figures, never forecasts.
